content:Speaker user says: I know, I know, the 2018/5779 High Holidays are over. But holidays are times when people recall incidents from years past, and not long after Rosh Hashanah this year I heard a charming 50-year-old holiday story from a most unlikely source. I wanted to put it on paper before it’s forgotten altogether. I love it because it is not only a story from a very different era, but it also includes the beautiful twist of a young woman’s “passing” as Jewish—a rare and unusual feat indeed!
Molly Roman is Irish-Catholic. Fifty years ago, she was a college freshman in Boston, living with three Jewish roommates. The freckle-faced redhead had never before set foot in a synagogue when Rosh Hashanah rolled around, and her friends asked her to accompany them to services. Why not go with them? they asked. She could think of no good reason, and so she accepted.
She doesn’t recall the name of the synagogue, but Molly remembers that it was lovely inside and out—which is really a compliment coming from someone brought up among ornate Catholic churches. She was thoroughly enjoying the Hebrew chants and the shofar blasts of the Rosh Hashanah morning service. Then, to her dismay, she began to hear whispering coming from the seats behind her.
At first, Molly tried to ignore the noise. But after a while she was so distracted and irritated that she turned around and shot the people behind her an angry look. A formidable woman even then, Molly apparently scowled in such a way that her neighbors immediately fell silent.
After the service, Molly and her friends rose to leave, along with the rest of the congregation. She had forgotten all about the interruption. It was then that one of the worshippers who had been sitting behind her touched her arm.
“Excuse me,” the man said, “I just wanted to apologize for making noise before. You see, this is my friends’ first synagogue service, and I was explaining to them what was going on.
And I am positively certain that he never dared.

Rosh Hashanah is one of the most significant holidays in the Jewish faith. It marks the beginning of the Jewish New Year and is traditionally a time for self-reflection, repentance, and renewal. 

The holiday usually falls in September or October and is observed over two days. During this time, Jews participate in synagogue services, pray, and may engage in fasting and other religious rituals. It is customary to hear the shofar, a hollowed-out ram's horn, which is blown in synagogues to signify the start of the new year. 

Rosh Hashanah is also called the Day of Judgment, as it is believed that God reviews the deeds of every individual and decides their fate for the coming year. Jews seek to repent for their sins and ask for forgiveness during this time, which is why it is often called the "Days of Awe."

With each flick of his wrist, a ka-boom echoed through the empty Webster Bank Arena, where Welsh and the Dutchmen face Michigan State on Friday in the first round of the NCAA tournament.
This has been Welsh's favorite pastime since he was a young boy growing up on his family's fourth-generation, 150-acre farm in Bayfield, Ontario, on the banks of Lake Huron.
One year Welsh's father, Ralph, built a big barn for all the farm equipment, the tractors and plows and the like. Though it wasn't exactly the plan, the barn proved fortuitous in Welsh's development as a hockey player.
"Every day after school I'd come home, go in there and shoot pucks," Welsh said. "I did it thousands and thousands of times."
Union would love to see its junior center fire more and more shots while wearing the garnet jersey, but one of the subplots of the Dutchmen's postseason will be whether that comes to fruition.
In fact, the question has been hanging over the Dutchmen most of the year: What happens to the guy they call "Welshie" when the season ends?
After the Dutchmen dispatched Havard in the ECAC championship game, Welsh changed into his suit and tie before most players had so much as unlaced their skates.
Why? Well, perhaps because Chicago Blackhawks general manager Stan Bowman was standing outside waiting to speak with him.
Welsh declined to comment on their conversation, but he acknowledged knowing there have been a handful of professional scouts at Union games all year. It seems inevitable Welsh will have a chance to turn pro sometime in the next few weeks.
"The good thing is no decisions have to be made right now," Welsh said, and that is indeed good for Union, because the Dutchmen need their 6-foot-3, 205-pound center if this historic season is to include a trip to Tampa, Fla., for the Frozen Four.
Welsh already has broken the program's single-season scoring record with 25 goals, and he centers the line that includes Daniel Carr and Josh Jooris.

Welsh shifted back to center his sophomore year and put in extra time with Union coach Rick Bennett, then an assistant, watching film. His goal production hopped from 10 his freshman year to 16 his sophomore year to 25 and counting this season.

2. Cardiovascular training: They engage in high-intensity interval training to improve their endurance and stamina.
3. Agility and speed training: They work on their footwork, balance, and speed through drills like ladder drills, cone drills, and plyometric exercises.
4. Stretching: They incorporate stretching and yoga to improve flexibility and prevent injuries.

Diet plan:
1. Lean protein: They consume lean proteins like chicken, fish, turkey, and eggs to build and repair muscle.
2. Complex carbohydrates: They eat whole grains, fruits, and vegetables to fuel their workouts and provide sustained energy.
3. Healthy fats: They consume healthy fats like avocados, nuts, and olive oil to support brain health and hormone production.

content:Speaker user says: About the only thing Grand Forks, N.D., and Boston have in common is their tradition of excellence in college hockey.
But the hockey styles of North Dakota and Boston University, who will face off at noon Saturday in the NCAA championship game at the Bradley Center, are as different as the lifestyles in their cities.
North Dakota plays the skating game, while Boston University thrives on power hitting.
"When we play our best, we make people pay when they touch the puck," said BU coach Jack Parker.
Michigan, the defending national champion and the top team in the polls for all but one week of the season, had to pay in Thursday's semifinals and went bankrupt. The Wolverines were beaten by BU 3-2 in a resounding upset.
"We can expect the same thing," said North Dakota's 5-foot-7-inch, 147-pound left wing Dave Hoogsteen, who leads the team in goals with 25. "We've got to pass the puck a lot and break to the open spot."
That's just what North Dakota did in whizzing by Colorado College 6-3 in the other semifinal.
"That was one of our best games of the year," said coach Dean Blais. "We don't have a lot of checkers. We're a puck-movement team that skates and passes."
The finalists met twice earlier in the season when Boston University took a late December trip to Grand Forks. BU lost the first game 6-4 and tied the second 2-2.
"Nobody did to us what North Dakota did to us out there," said Parker. "In the second game we did figure out a way to stop them a little bit--we just had Michel Larocque make 47 saves. We certainly cannot play that kind of hockey Saturday against North Dakota and expect to win.
"They present a different look than Michigan and pose different problems. They have a lot of little forwards who can beat defensemen on the give-and-go coming out of the corners. Quickness and speed are two different things, and they have both of them."
While balanced scoring is North Dakota's forte, BU boasts the most dynamic individual in the championship game, Chris Drury, a junior center with 38 goals. In Blais' opinion: "He's the best player in the tournament. Brendan Morrison (of Michigan) is the Hobey Baker Award winner, but Drury outplayed him Thursday night.
"We're fortunate in having the last line change so we can put our best defensive line--Adam Calder, Matt Henderson and Jeff Ulmer--on Drury's line."

content:Speaker user says: What inspired torukmakto4 to become a Nerf hobbyist and how does their approach differ from others in the Nerf community?
Generate according to: The Dart Zone: So this is how it begins.
>> So who the hell is this torukmakto4?
Well, this place is called The Dart Zone for a reason, isn't it? Among other things, I'm a nerf hobbyist. Just like Bazookafied, MyLastDart, Randomshadow, Bobololo and all the various authors of NM&R over the years.
Or, perhaps you remember my name because you hate my guts.
The long and short of it, though, is that I'm just an ordinary guy. College student, HVZ player... I do this for fun. It's a hobby. There is no commercial interest here. I play games and I try to further and advance what we do, and I try to get my ideas out there for what they are worth.
Another tidbit about me... Blogger MyLastDart recently blogged about blogging, about how not to fall into the endless field of sameness that a lot of blogs end up part of. In short, you need an angle. You need a position and a character all your own. There are too many people spamming, I agree. Endless reposting, low quality reactions to other bloggers. Ugh.
What I realized? Man, do I have an angle. I should post something, shouldn't I?
Yeah, The Dart Zone. Just a name. Doesn't really mean anything special. It's a zone... For stuff that shoots darts.
There were enough "Nerf _________" and "__________ Nerf" blog titles out there. Aside from Nerf Mods And Reviews, I find most of those just don't... Ring.
The Dart Zone. I like it. I think I'll keep it.
I'll get in the habit of calling it DZ.
Anyway, back to angles. But first, a little history of where torukmakto4 came from.
Back in early 2010, I was a senior in high school. Humans vs. Zombies and the whole idea of nerf being a hobby was completely unknown to me. Hell, nerf was completely unknown to me. Then... Everything changed. One day, Lockheed Martin reps showed up to our class talking about some kind of robotics competition. I was in, almost as a matter of course... The task? Run a timed target shoot with RC vehicles on a course going head-to-head with other teams. We had to have large projectiles to retrieve and count for scoring, which were safe for bystanders in case of accident, and carried enough momentum to knock down the targets. It was made for nerf. So, my team rolled out a winning bot, based on a cheap toy-grade RC tank with new electronics and, most importantly, a prominent electrically primed Nerf Raider on a simple low-cost elevating mount I conceived.
I ended up fabricating a lot of parts for that, and not to grab credit, but my parts were about half of our eventual victory. The other half? It was our winning weapons choices, a solid, reliable gun tuned to the edge of permitted power with an accurate mount system and a huge magazine. Others missed, jammed and failed to knock down targets with their Tommy 20 and burned off whole cans of ammo with their Vulcans, we just steadily click-click-boom'ed our way to victory.
So what's this tangent about robots and high school have to do with DZ?
Well, all I am doing now as I mod and play HVZ is precisely what I did years ago for that competition. I owe my entire philosophy and approach to the "Lockheed Bot". I am perfectly unchanged from then; I am just analyzing practical applications for nerf guns - games like HVZ - and designing and modding my way to performance in those applications. It's very cold and hard and one-sided to me.
I didn't have any nerf guns as a child and was only dimly aware of their existence back then in 2010, and that would prove to be the key to everything. That damn robot, it was my first contact. Wrenching on that thing got me into nerf, rather than the other way around. That is what sets me apart from a lot of nerfers, I find. I have no preconceptions, no prejudices. I look at nerf and I do not see toys, nor childhood memories, nor something to unwind and turn off my brain with. I am not going to limit what I do with nerf to these, or any other arbitrary idea of "what nerf is supposed to be". I look at nerf and I see tools. Means to ends. Equipment with certain attributes that make them work for certain uses; say, simulating firearms in an on-campus reenactment of a zombie apocalypse.
And, I see fun stuff. VERY COOL stuff, to buy, design, work on, improve and use.

content:Speaker assistant says: Sure! Here are some tips for beginner surfers:

1. Choose the right beginner surfboard: Look for a large, stable soft-top surfboard with plenty of foam to provide buoyancy and stability. This type of board will be easier to paddle and stand on as a beginner.

2. Start in small waves: Look for gentle waves with a small swell, and practice in knee-high waves. This will help you get comfortable with balancing and paddling.

3. Paddle properly: Paddling is key to catching waves. Place your hands flat on the board, and paddle with long, smooth strokes, keeping your elbows bent.

4. Practice standing up: Start by practicing standing up on the beach. Lie down on the board, and when you feel a wave push you, plant your hands on either side of your chest and pop up to your feet.

5. Always look where you’re going: Keep your eyes on the horizon and look where you want to go, not at the board or your feet. This will help you stay balanced and ride the wave more smoothly.

6. Stay safe: Always surf in a designated area with lifeguards on duty, and be aware of other surfers and hazards like rocks, rip tides, or sharks.

With patience, practice, and a positive attitude, you can become a confident and capable surfer.
